title: Mobile app permissions and side-loaded apps
body_md:
## Treat a permission as access, not a verdict

A phone app can request the camera, microphone, location, contacts, photos or notifications because a feature needs them. The same grant can expose information beyond the task you intended. Ask three questions: **What feature needs this? Does it need access now or only while I use the feature? What happens if I decline?** A map needs location for directions; a wallpaper app normally does not need your contacts. An odd request is a reason to investigate, not proof of malware.

On iPhone, Settings → Privacy & Security lists apps by data type; you can grant or revoke access. On Android, Settings → Security & privacy/Privacy → Privacy dashboard shows recent use on supported versions, then lets you inspect permissions. Some apps present an additional in-app permission or cloud-sharing setting: changing the OS grant may not remove data already uploaded. Review the app's account settings too. Denying a legitimate permission may disable one feature; try the narrowest option offered, such as selected photos, approximate location or access only while using the app. Reopen the feature and see whether it still works.

## Off-store installation is a separate decision

On Android an APK from a message or website bypasses the normal Play Store install path. Google Play Protect also scans apps from other sources, but a clean scan is not a guarantee. A warning asking you to disable scanning, grant Accessibility, read notifications or install another package deserves a stop. These powers can let an app observe or act on sensitive screens. Obtain the app from the publisher's independently found official channel and verify why its distribution differs; if the source or need is unclear, postpone installation. Do not follow a link supplied by an unexpected caller.

Apple's alternative distribution rules differ by region and OS. Do not assume that every iPhone can install arbitrary apps, or that the App Store or any alternative store eliminates malicious behavior. Device management profiles and enterprise distribution deserve the same independent verification. If work or school manages the phone, ask its administrator before removing required controls.

## A workable review cycle

Start with high-impact grants: contacts, notification access, accessibility, precise/background location, microphone, camera and full photo library. For each app, identify the real feature and publisher, reduce the grant where possible, then test the feature. Uninstall an app you no longer need and remove its account access separately if applicable. Keep the OS and apps updated. If you already installed a suspicious package, stop using it, remove its permissions and the app through system settings, on Android run Play Protect, and review accounts used on that phone from a trusted device. A reset or provider help may be needed if it had powerful device-control access; the exact recovery depends on the device.

widget_config.goal: Audit one phone app by matching each permission to a feature, then decide safely whether an off-store install is necessary.
widget_config.today_action: Open the system permission list, review one app you no longer use and one that handles photos or messages, and revoke access that has no current purpose. On Android, confirm Play Protect is on.
widget_config.scope: General Android/iOS guidance as of 2026-10-20; menu names and alternative app distribution vary by OS, device, country and store policy. Permissions and store review reduce risk but do not certify an app.

blocks.title: The urgent delivery APK
blocks.situation: A fictional courier message says a parcel will be lost unless Mira installs “ParcelTrack.apk” and enables notification access. The link and parcel are synthetic.
blocks.analysis: The requested power is unrelated to viewing a parcel. Notification access can reveal verification messages. Mira checks her orders in the retailer app she already uses and asks the courier via its known channel; she does not install the file. A real delivery could still exist, so she verifies the order rather than dismissing it.

blocks.title: The scan button that needs a camera
blocks.situation: A known banking app asks for camera access only when Leon taps “scan document”. It offers limited photo selection too.
blocks.analysis: The timing and feature make camera access plausible. Leon grants access while using the app, checks the document is sent to the expected bank workflow, and later revokes it if unused. Permission alone does not prove the app or destination is genuine.

blocks.title: Choose settings for a family phone
blocks.setup: Synthetic practice: a relative wants a parcel tracker and a photo-scanning app. No real package, code or account data is entered.

steps.prompt: A text offers a tracker APK and says Play Protect must be turned off. What first?

choices.text: Open the known retailer app or type its known address independently.
choices.consequence: You can check the order without granting a stranger install rights.
choices.explanation: Independent navigation separates the real service from the message.

choices.text: Turn off Play Protect and install the APK.
choices.consequence: The package may gain powerful access before you verify its publisher.
choices.explanation: Pressure and a request to disable a safeguard are strong reasons to stop.

steps.prompt: A known scanner asks for all photos when you need one image.

choices.consequence: Unrelated photos become accessible to the app.
choices.explanation: A convenient default is broader than this one-image need.

choices.text: Use selected-photo access if available, then test scanning.
choices.consequence: The feature works with less exposure.
choices.explanation: Grant the minimum needed for the current task.

steps.prompt: The scanner now asks for microphone access although you only scan paper.

choices.text: Decline and check whether the scan still works; investigate any voice feature later.
choices.consequence: The scan can continue if audio is unnecessary.
choices.explanation: A permission should follow a feature, not the mere presence of a prompt.

choices.text: Allow because the app is in a store.
choices.consequence: Store review does not explain or limit this grant.
choices.explanation: Distribution is one signal, not a reason to approve every request.

steps.prompt: The relative says the tracker was installed last week and has notification access.

choices.text: Leave it because nothing bad has happened visibly.
choices.consequence: The app keeps receiving future notifications.
choices.explanation: Absence of a visible loss does not make unnecessary access safe.

choices.text: Revoke the access, uninstall the suspect app, and review affected accounts from a trusted device.
choices.consequence: Exposure stops and you can investigate what happened.
choices.explanation: Revoking now cannot undo prior access, so account review matters.

blocks.debrief: Replay the four decisions using this rule: verify the publisher independently, grant the smallest functional permission, and investigate past access separately.

questions.prompt: A familiar map requests location only when directions start. Best response?

choices.text: Allow while using the app and review later.
choices.explanation: The permission matches the feature without permanent background access.

choices.text: Never allow location to any app.
choices.explanation: That disables a legitimate route feature unnecessarily.
That is broader than this trip requires.

questions.prompt: After you revoke contacts, an app’s address-book feature works worse. What does that prove?

choices.explanation: A broken feature alone cannot establish malicious intent.

choices.text: Only that this feature may need contacts; check what it does and who publishes the app.
choices.explanation: Denying a legitimate permission can affect a feature; it is not a malware test.

questions.prompt: Play Protect reports no issue with an unknown APK. What follows?

choices.text: Continue independent publisher and need checks; scanning is partial.
choices.explanation: A scan can miss new or deceptive behavior.

choices.text: It is proven safe to grant Accessibility.
choices.explanation: A clean result is not certification for powerful access.

questions.prompt: After uninstalling an app, what may still need attention?

choices.text: Its cloud account access and data already uploaded.
choices.explanation: Uninstalling stops local app use but cannot automatically erase remote copies.
